extracted.intended_audience: researchers and policymakers studying gender and equity in grant funding, higher-education researchers, and research-methods scholars
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing gender bias in grant funding
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and interpreting research on applicant gender and grant-peer-review outcomes, and recommendations for policy/practice to reduce gendered inequities in grant funding. Focuses on methodological choices, necessary controls, and institutional interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for sub‑field acceptance rates / application rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Control for acceptance rate within each sub‑field because female applicants may apply disproportionately to more competitive fields (e.g. medical and social sciences) while male applicants apply to less competitive fields (e.g. physics). When this is statistically controlled, apparent gender differences may disappear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stratify or control analyses by sub‑field acceptance rates and application patterns to avoid Simpson’s paradox and spurious gender effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratify datasets by critical variables (application rate, academic rank, field)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stratifying datasets according to critical variables such as application rate, applicants’ academic rank, and academic field may be insightful for understanding gender differences in funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report analyses stratified (or include interaction terms) for these variables rather than only reporting aggregate gender comparisons; cite examples (Boyle et al., Holliday et al., Pohlhaus et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardise evaluation criteria in grant peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant funding peer reviews do not necessarily have standardised criteria—grant schemes and reviewers may have different benchmarks about what constitutes merit or being worthy of investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For research and policy, push for clearer, standardised evaluation criteria across schemes or explicitly document scheme-specific criteria when comparing results across contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify evaluation criteria and their order of priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Special attention should be given to clarifying the evaluation criteria and the order of their priority used to measure applicants’ performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which criteria are primary vs secondary in decision-making and make this explicit in study design and in institutional evaluation guidance; this helps reveal where bias may enter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent operationalisation of applicant productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant academic productivity has been conceptualised through different bibliometric measures: single normalised impact factors, indices, or composites (e.g. h‑index + sum of impact factors + past funding experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which productivity measures are used; consider comprehensive/composite indices when possible; report limitations and justification for chosen metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include productivity and performance measures where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Some studies do not consider productivity measures (due to lack of access, perceived unimportance, or feasibility), but failure to account for these co‑occurring variables can lead to spurious results regarding applicant gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and include measurable performance indicators where possible, or state explicitly when they are missing and discuss likely bias from omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify research goals: examine processes as well as outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies differ in goals—some examine gender disparities in funding decisions, others examine the peer review process that leads to those decisions. Focusing on only one may occlude interactions between variables contributing to the broader context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design research to probe both the review process (e.g. critique language, scoring) and final funding outcomes to identify sources of disparities, not just their existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for systemic and structural biases beyond reviewer behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender disparities may arise from structural problems inherent in academia (e.g. women-to-men ratio in senior positions, institutional family support) that affect funding outcomes independently of reviewer bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include institutional-level and career-trajectory variables (faculty composition, promotion structures, resource allocation) in analyses and policy responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify how each evaluation criterion may be prone to gender bias (individual/systemic/societal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should identify how each of the evaluation criteria may be prone to gender bias at an individual, systemic, and/or societal level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map evaluation criteria onto potential bias mechanisms (e.g. stereotypes affecting judgments of applicant quality) and test susceptibility empirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include life-course and employment situation variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Elucidating how one’s life course and employment situation can indirectly impact academic performance will be essential — address family situations, employment status (teaching load, precarity), and institutional support (research resources, promotion services).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect variables such as caregiving responsibilities, teaching/admin loads, contract type, and access to institutional support to model pre‑submission disadvantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider intersectionality (race, age, religion, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond gender, other diversity-related factors such as race, age, and religion may bring about cumulative disadvantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intersectional analyses to examine how multiple identity factors combine to affect funding outcomes and avoid attributing effects solely to gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate statistical controls to avoid spurious results
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to account for co‑occurring variables can lead to spurious results regarding the effect of applicant gender; most studies have made efforts to account for extraneous variables though not exhaustively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include relevant covariates, justify model specifications, test robustness to alternative operationalisations, and be cautious about over‑ or under‑controlling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and plan for inevitable variation across studies and contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Variation across studies is inevitable because review contexts differ; this may lead to studies operationalising concepts differently or setting distinct research goals, resulting in case‑like studies that are difficult to generalise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When synthesising evidence, document heterogeneity in operationalisation and context; use meta‑analytic or multilevel approaches when possible to aggregate across differing designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate reviewer-level bias from pre‑submission structural bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential challenges female researchers face are engrained at two levels: biases emerging during specific peer review contexts, and biases that impact the researcher prior to submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design studies and interventions that separately measure in-review biases (e.g. critique language, scores) and pre-existing career disadvantages (e.g. publication record influenced by caregiving).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve reviewer training to enhance inter‑rater reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Training opportunities could be more actively introduced to refine the quality of reviewers’ assessments and inter‑rater reliability (Sattler et al., 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement and evaluate reviewer calibration/training programs and measure their effects on score consistency and bias indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement blinded / anonymized review measures where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: While difficulties remain in anonymising applicants’ identities entirely, measures to implement a blinded review may result in providing more equal and reliable reviews (example: NSF’s experimentation with anonymized review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pilot and evaluate partial or full anonymization procedures, report feasibility limitations, and measure impacts on gender disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt institutional interventions to remove structural and cultural obstacles
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional strategies should include promoting the retention of female researchers (appointing more women to higher positions), relieving them of teaching and administrative responsibilities, and increasing permanent positions or funding schemes dedicated to female researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test and evaluate targeted institutional policies (hiring, workload adjustments, dedicated funding) for effects on career progression and funding success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote mentoring and awareness-raising as individual-level interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentoring is shown to be effective in promoting both practical and emotional support in the academic context, leading participants to obtain greater research funding, higher publication rates, and better self-perceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement mentoring programs, monitor outcomes for mentees (funding, productivity, retention), and include such supports in evaluations of equity initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political and policy action to change institutional practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Political efforts need to take shape to shift the status quo of institutional practices and trends that perpetuate gender inequities in academia and funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate for policy levers (funding agency rules, reporting requirements, equity audits) and evaluate their downstream effects on applicant experiences and outcomes.
